title: Flies and Lightning

patient.name: Mr Tan Wei Ming
patient.presenting_complaint: Sudden new floaters and flashes of light in the right eye for the past two days
patient.address: Blk 784 Ang Mo Kio Ave 3, #06-058, Singapore 140861

history.hpc: Mr Tan reports new symptoms in the right eye for two days. He says: 'Suddenly I see like got black flies floating, and sometimes flash flash like lightning at the corner.' He is highly myopic and wears thick glasses. He denies a curtain or shadow over his vision so far, no pain, no redness. He is worried because it came on suddenly.
history.pmhx: High myopia (about -8.00 both eyes). No previous eye surgery or trauma.
history.social_hx: Lorry driver — vision important for work. Non-smoker.

examination_findings.fundus: Requires dilated examination by doctor (high-risk symptoms in a myope) — to be arranged

investigations.history_documentation: Targeted ocular history obtained: onset (sudden, 2 days), nature (floaters described as black flies, flashes like lightning), laterality (right eye), absence of a curtain/shadow so far, high myopia, family history of retinal detachment, no prior surgery/trauma. These features raise concern for a retinal tear/detachment risk and warrant prompt dilated review.

diagnosis: New flashes and floaters in a high myope with a family history of retinal detachment — history features that warrant urgent dilated fundus examination by the doctor to exclude a retinal tear/detachment. The competency is taking a focused, red-flag-aware history and escalating appropriately.

immediate: Take a focused ocular history: sudden vs gradual, one or both eyes, nature of floaters and flashes
Specifically ask about a curtain/shadow or field loss (red flag for detachment) and document its absence/presence
Note high myopia and the family history of retinal detachment as risk factors
Recognise these as red-flag symptoms and inform the doctor/nurse promptly for a dilated examination
Perform baseline VA and IOP and document the history clearly
Do not reassure the patient that it is nothing — escalate for assessment
follow_up: Doctor to perform a dilated fundus examination to look for a retinal tear/detachment
Arrange dilation as ordered and prepare the patient for it
Advise urgent return if a curtain/shadow, worsening floaters, or vision loss develops
patient_education: Explain that sudden flashes and floaters need to be checked, especially with his short-sightedness and family history
Tell him the warning sign to watch for: a dark curtain or shadow coming across the vision
Advise him to return immediately if that happens, and to avoid heavy straining meanwhile
Reassure him that prompt checking is precautionary and important for his eye and his driving job

key_points: Establishes onset (sudden), laterality (right), and nature of floaters/flashes
Specifically asks about a curtain/shadow or field loss (detachment red flag)
Identifies high myopia and family history of retinal detachment as risk factors
Confirms no pain/redness and no prior surgery/trauma
Documents the focused ocular history accurately
Recognises the symptoms require a dilated fundus examination
Records the risk factors clearly for the doctor
Recognises flashes/floaters in a myope with family history as high-risk
Knows these features warrant prompt dilated review to exclude retinal tear/detachment
Identifies the curtain/shadow as the key escalation red flag
Does not falsely reassure the patient
Escalates promptly to the doctor/nurse for dilated examination
Prepares the patient for dilation and documents the history
Gives clear red-flag advice (curtain/shadow) and when to return urgently
Communicates supportively without dismissing the symptoms
